Who is there

Everyone comes with a purpose

  • networking up
  • meeting coauthors
  • bonding with groups
  • gaining visibility

You only get what you put in. Going without an aim is not worth much.

Benefit: a reason to finish and to practise

Deadlines

  • A yearly deadline gets you to submit
  • AOM and SMS: you can review papers
  • Rare for students

Presenting

  • A skill that takes practice
  • Watch strong presentations
  • Learn from them and copy what works

Benefit: finding your room

Which room do you belong to?

  • AOM and SMS have many rooms
  • Early on: follow general interest
  • Organic, spontaneous
  • Where do you focus?
  • Whose people do you want to meet?
  • Match faces to surnames you read

My rooms

  • Open source, user innovation
  • A bit of platforms, a bit of geopolitics
  • AI is everywhere

Benefit: people

Peers

  • Students at stronger schools
  • Similar interests
  • A year ahead of you
  • Young APs you share ties with
  • Let them lead the way

Core people

  • The pillars of your field
  • The gatekeepers
  • No need to force it

Beyond “say hi”

  • Present your work
  • Draw like-minded people
  • Get senior feedback
  • Ask good questions
  • Visible in small circles

First time strangers, second time friends

  • Over the years: a cohort, a support group, coauthors

Benefit: ideas and feedback

Why luck

  • A 15–20 minute talk rarely gets real feedback
  • PDWs help more: papers go in ahead
  • Everyone reads and comments on each other’s papers

Cost: time and money

A fixed research budget

Visa and immigration: cost and risk

Preparing, plus research time and classes you miss

The opportunity cost is real.

Cost: overexposure

Your ideas

  • Ideas not thought through
  • Papers not ready
  • Bigger conference, bigger risk of being scooped

Yourself

  • The audience may be your future hiring committee
  • Bad first impression: work, presentation style, offline talk
  • Can be worse than not showing up

The other side

  • A good first impression
  • Visibility over the years as you improve
  • A network for the job market and letters

Tricky.
I’m still exploring, learning, and making mistakes.

Part 3 · Gaming industry

User Feedback and Innovation Speed

Generative and corrective feedback, product modularity, and time to full release in Steam Early Access

Yupeng Liu and Ashton HawkWork in progress

Grand Theft Auto VI: late, twice

May 2025: first delay

November 2025: second delay

November 2025: investors react

Rockstar: the extra months let them “finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect.”

Promised for 2025, now November 2026. Take-Two shares fell sharply after the second delay.

Push Square, 2 May 2025; Engadget, 6 Nov 2025; Stockhouse, 7 Nov 2025; key art: Rockstar Games

Products are often late, and speed matters

Innovation speed

Time to market is a core outcome of innovation

  • Research on new products treats development speed as a main result.
  • Iteration and testing help projects finish faster.

 

Speed is a capability, and rushing is costly

  • Some firms finish comparable projects faster, year after year.
  • Doing the same work in less time costs more.

Why does a product take longer than planned? One reason: what counts as finished moves during development.

Eisenhardt & Tabrizi 1995; Kessler & Chakrabarti 1996; Dierickx & Cool 1989; Hawk, Pacheco-de-Almeida & Yeung 2013; Pacheco-de-Almeida, Hawk & Yeung 2015; Hawk & Pacheco-de-Almeida 2018

Building in front of users: Early Access

Steam, “What is Early Access?”, read 6 Nov 2026

Slay the Spire 2 store page (in Early Access since Mar 2026)

A studio sells an unfinished game, keeps updating it in front of paying players, and promises a finished version.

When the game leaves Early Access, that is the full release; developers call this version 1.0. Buyers get it as a free update.

In Early Access, user feedback arrives while the product is still in development.

Baldur's Gate 3

34 months in Early Access

October 2020 to full release in August 2023

97% positive

of about 760,000 Steam reviews

Players helped make a hit, and it took almost three years.

Steam store page, Baldur's Gate 3

The puzzle

User innovation

Users help firms innovate

  • Users know what a product lacks.
  • Firms that develop products with users innovate more.
  • User ideas can be more novel and more useful to customers than professionals’ ideas.

Recent work

But user input has costs

  • Firms that follow crowd suggestions get a narrower range of ideas afterward.
  • Customer participation during development slows time to market.

Prior work asks whether user input pays off. We ask which feedback helps a product get finished, and which delays it.

von Hippel 1994; Chatterji & Fabrizio 2014; Poetz & Schreier 2012; Park, Piezunka & Dahlander 2024; Chang & Taylor 2016

Research question

How does user feedback influence the speed of innovation: does it speed it up or slow it down?

How does product architecture change this effect?

Why Early Access fits the question

  • Players buy and play the game while it is still being built.
  • Players post reviews and developers post patch notes, all public and dated: 1.22M reviews and 334,817 developer posts for 4,793 games.
  • Players’ comments may push developers to add features and enlarge the scope.

Steam store pages, reviews and developer posts

What makes a product finish

A game reaches full release when the studio decides it is done. Two things set how long that takes.

Scope

How much is left to build

More work left means a longer time to full release (positive relationship).

Pace

How fast the studio works

A faster studio reaches full release sooner (negative relationship).

User feedback can affect both: it can expand scope or raise pace.

Eisenhardt & Tabrizi 1995; Hawk, Pacheco-de-Almeida & Yeung 2013

Two kinds of user feedback

Through Early Access, users can bring two types of information to game development.

Corrective feedbackGenerative feedback
ContentAn existing part falls short: bugs, balance, controlsSomething is missing: new content, systems, modes
SearchProblemistic search: usually ends once the problem is solvedSearch for new features: the end point is often unclear
When it arrivesAdds work within the current designAdds work beyond the current design
When addressedA fix moves the product closer to completionA new feature expands what the finished product includes
In reviews“I fell through the ground and had to restart.”
“The steering is too sensitive.”		“Please give us online pvp mode.”
“If they added … co-op to the dungeon mode and then PVP battles and looting to the Arena mode …”

von Hippel 1994; Cyert & March 1963

H1: Generative feedback delays completion

H1

The more generative feedback a product receives during development, the longer its time to full release.

  • Generative feedback concerns features the game does not yet have.
  • Each request that is adopted expands the scope of the finished product.
  • Generative search often lacks a clear stopping point: each new feature can prompt further requests.

H2: Responding to corrective feedback speeds completion

H2

The more a firm responds to corrective feedback during development, the shorter its time to full release.

  • Corrective feedback concerns existing parts that fall short.
  • Each fix brings the product closer to completion.
  • Problemistic search usually ends once the problem is solved.

Cyert & March 1963

Product modularity: how far a change travels

A product is modular when it is built from parts that can be changed one at a time.

Change propagation: a change in one part forces changes in other parts. The more modular the product, the less a change propagates.

Modular game
Add a new weapon → the rest of the game still works.
Fix one weapon → nothing else breaks.

Integral game
Add a new chapter → later chapters must change.
Fix one scene → a quest elsewhere can break.

Simon 1962; Ulrich 1995; Baldwin & Clark 2000; Eckert, Clarkson & Zanker 2004

H3a: Modularity amplifies the delay

H3a

Product modularity strengthens the positive relationship between generative feedback and time to full release.

  • Pace: each addition plugs in without touching other parts, so it is built faster.
  • Scope: when each addition is cheap and low-risk, saying yes costs less, so the planned scope can keep growing.
  • The two forces pull in opposite directions. Requests often lack a clear end point, so the scope force tends to dominate.

Ulrich 1995; Baldwin & Clark 2000

H3b: Modularity amplifies the speed-up

H3b

Product modularity strengthens the negative relationship between responsiveness to corrective feedback and time to full release.

  • Pace: a fix stays inside one part, so it is done faster.
  • Scope: a local fix breaks fewer other parts, so it creates fewer new problems.
  • The two forces point in the same direction. Fixes usually have a clear end point, so both forces speed completion.

Ethiraj & Levinthal 2004; MacCormack, Rusnak & Baldwin 2006

Summary of the argument

User feedback → design changes → how far each change travels → scope and pace → time to full release.

Modularity makes both links stronger: requests delay the game more, and fixes speed it up more.

Measuring the two kinds of feedback

Classifier: TF-IDF text features and logistic regression, one model per label, trained on 1,200 Early Access reviews labeled by an LLM, then applied to all 1.22M reviews. A review can carry more than one label. Exposure pools all reviews from the three months before month t (at least 5 text reviews).

Steam player reviews

Measuring responsiveness to corrective feedback

For each update post: similarity between its notes and the game’s corrective reviews from the previous 90 days. Game-month value: mean over all update posts from Early Access entry up to the month before t, standardized.

Review and update texts in the sketch are illustrative.

Steam player reviews and developer update posts

Measuring product modularity

Each Steam game shows up to 20 tags. Tags are applied and voted on by Steam users; the list is ranked by votes.

Recombinable tags: Sandbox, Survival, Crafting, Base Building, Colony Sim, Automation, City Builder, Roguelike, Roguelite, Procedural Generation, Deckbuilding, Open World Survival Craft, Roguelike Deckbuilder

Sequenced tags: Story Rich, Linear, Narrative, Choices Matter, Visual Novel, Walking Simulator, Point & Click, Cinematic, Puzzle, Metroidvania

Modularity = share of tag votes on recombinable tags − share on sequenced tags (then standardized)

ValheimBaldur’s Gate 3
(1) Share of tag votes on recombinable tags30%0%
(2) Share of tag votes on sequenced tags0%14%
Modularity index = (1) − (2)+0.30 (high)−0.14 (low)

Alternative measures: narrow tag index; recombinable tag in the top five; number of Workshop creators; month of the first Workshop item.

Empirical model

  • Outcome: in each month a game is still in Early Access, does it make its full release that month? About 3% of game-months do (2,144 releases in 74,013 game-months, 3,509 games).
  • Baseline: the release chance can differ by Early Access age (0–2, 3–5, 6–8, 9–11, 12–17, 18–23, 24–35, 36–47, 48+ months), and this age pattern can change with modularity. It also differs by entry year and calendar month. Controls include genre, multiplayer, price, publisher, developer experience, review volume and tone, and update frequency.
  • Reading the signs: a negative coefficient means a lower chance of full release in a given month, so a longer time to full release.

Discrete-time logit hazard; standard errors clustered by game

Modularity moderates both

More feature requests lower the chance of full release in more modular games (3.5% → 2.4%) and barely change it in less modular games.

Responding to corrective feedback raises the chance more in more modular games (2.2% → 3.8%) than in less modular ones (2.6% → 3.2%).

Predicted chance of full release in a given month, from the model in the results table, at the sample average (2.9%); more modular = +1 SD, less modular = −1 SD.

Mechanism: does a change spread?

  • We take every pair of back-to-back updates by the same game during Early Access (88,925 pairs, 3,253 games); each pair is analyzed once for each of 11 game parts.
  • We sort each patch-note item by the part of the game it touches (combat, interface, economy, map, …).
  • We ask: when an update changes some parts, how likely is the next update to fix bugs in other parts?

How the mechanism test works

  1. 1. Data. 88,925 pairs of back-to-back updates (at most 60 days apart) from 3,253 Early Access games.
  2. 2. Coding. Keyword rules assign each patch-note item to the game parts it touches (11 parts: combat, interface, economy, map, …) and mark it if it is a bug fix.
  3. 3. Outcome. For each part, does the next update fix a bug in it? On average, 15.5% do.
  4. 4. Comparison. We relate this to how many other parts the first update changed, and ask whether the link differs with modularity. We compare updates within the same game and hold update size fixed.

Result: in more modular games, changes in other parts are followed by fewer bug fixes in a given part (interaction −0.0011 per part changed, per SD of modularity; p = .007).

Developer update posts on Steam; linear probability model with game and part fixed effects, standard errors clustered by game

Are delays punished?

Launch performance of 1,643 games that reached full release, compared with games that never announced a date:

Positive reviews, first 3 monthsReviews, first 3 months (log)
Delayed after announcing a date (79)+3.6 points, p = .011+0.53, p < .001
Launched on the announced date (134)+3.2 points, p = .003+0.35, p < .001
Delayed minus on time+0.4 points, p = .83+0.18, p = .31

Delays are not punished. Games that delay do as well as games that launch on their announced date.

Steam reviews in the first three months after full release; controls measured early in Early Access

Does finishing faster cost quality?

Speed: time in Early Access relative to the time expected for a comparable game.

Finishing faster or slower than expected is not related to review positivity after release

1,643 Early Access games that reached full release; positive-review share in the first three months: about −0.7 points per SD of speed, not significant; all estimates within ±2 points.

No evidence of a speed–quality trade-off at full release.

Cohen, Eliashberg & Ho 1996; Bayus 1997; Hawk & Pacheco-de-Almeida 2018; Hawk, Pacheco-de-Almeida & Yeung 2013

Contribution

User innovation

User feedback can slow development as well as speed it

Feature requests are associated with a longer time to full release; responding to bug and design complaints, with a shorter one.

Modularity

Modularity strengthens both effects

In more modular games, feature requests delay full release more, and responding to complaints speeds it up more.

Innovation speed

Users change how much there is to build

Work on innovation speed mostly studies how fast firms work. User feedback also changes the scope of the product, and with it the time to completion.

von Hippel 1994; Chang & Taylor 2016; Hawk, Pacheco-de-Almeida & Yeung 2013
